records.hook: Australia deserves more than one famous skyline.

sections.title: Historical landscapes
sections.body: Australia deserves more than one famous skyline. Around the continent are tropical reefs, desert landscapes, temperate forests, vast coastal regions and cities with very different histories. The Great Barrier Reef is an especially strong example of why the natural environment and human heritage should be explored together.

sections.title: Nature and conservation
sections.body: UNESCO recognises the Reef as a large and varied marine ecosystem. Coral habitat and water quality face pressures connected to warming oceans, while inland landscapes have very different ecological processes. A balanced Australian atlas also needs interior and northern places, not only Sydney, Melbourne and the beaches.

sections.title: Living cultures
sections.body: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples maintain cultural relationships to land and Sea Country, including the Reef region. The Reef Authority specifically recognises ongoing Traditional Owner management and knowledge. Cultural interpretation must respect local communities’ own stories and avoid treating all First Nations traditions as interchangeable.

sections.title: A continent of different stories
sections.body: The Reef alone extends across many different seascapes and Traditional Owner connections. Inland, the experience of Country changes from desert to grassland to wooded ranges, so a generic paragraph about beaches misses much of Australia. The country’s historic and contemporary cultural life is not a single story either: First Nations histories, migrations and modern cities all matter. The Great Barrier Reef is a useful opening chapter, not a substitute for understanding the continent.

records.quickFact: The Great Barrier Reef is an entire marine region, not a single reef — and its Sea Country has continuing Traditional Owner custodians.

records.hook: The Central African Republic is often missing from general travel atlases, which means its landscapes and cultures are too easily overlooked.

sections.title: Historical landscapes
sections.body: The Central African Republic is often missing from general travel atlases, which means its landscapes and cultures are too easily overlooked. The Sangha Trinational World Heritage landscape links this country with neighbouring Cameroon and the Republic of the Congo in a shared conservation area.

sections.title: Nature and conservation
sections.body: Dzanga-Sangha’s forest clearings are famous for gatherings of forest elephants. The surrounding ecosystems also support other rare wildlife. This is a region of high biodiversity and complex conservation needs; describing it purely as an animal-viewing destination would overlook local communities and the forest’s changing ecological relationships.

sections.title: Living cultures
sections.body: The country’s cultural life includes Sango and a range of other languages and traditions. Its wider history, music and social realities require careful, sourced treatment. Even when one protected reserve makes an unforgettable first impression, the country deserves more than a single nature photograph.

sections.title: People inside the conservation picture
sections.body: It is tempting to describe Dzanga-Sangha as a remote forest where wildlife takes centre stage. Yet conservation decisions also affect local livelihoods, access and knowledge, and the broader Sangha landscape crosses national borders. Indigenous forest communities have longstanding cultural relationships with these environments. The reserve’s elephants are memorable, but a responsible account also recognises how people live alongside animals and how difficult it can be to protect habitat under social and economic pressure.

records.quickFact: The Sangha Trinational forest crosses the borders of three countries; the wildlife does not recognise the lines drawn on a map.

records.hook: Cameroon has both forest and mountain heritage.

sections.title: Historical landscapes
sections.body: Cameroon has both forest and mountain heritage. UNESCO recognises the Dja Faunal Reserve, the shared Sangha forest landscape, and the Diy-Gid-Biy cultural landscape of the Mandara Mountains. These are very different environments, and together they challenge any attempt to define the whole country through a single photograph.

sections.title: Nature and conservation
sections.body: The Congo Basin forests of southern Cameroon support elephants, apes, rich plant life and communities with detailed knowledge of the environment. The Dja River curves around much of the protected reserve. Conservation here involves both biodiversity and questions about how neighbouring communities take part in decisions.

sections.title: Living cultures
sections.body: Cameroon also contains sharply varied languages, cultural traditions and landscapes beyond these protected areas. Learning about it means moving from forest communities to cities and mountains, and acknowledging the voices of people who actually live there rather than treating a UNESCO label as the whole story.

sections.title: The landscape beyond a single park
sections.body: A map pin in Yaoundé cannot represent all of Cameroon. The north, the western highlands and the humid southern forests differ profoundly in climate and cultural history. River catchments and mountain ranges influence travel, farming and settlement as much as they influence wildlife. Dja is one important protected landscape, but the country’s wider mixture of environments explains why a profile must connect conservation to people, languages, towns and the everyday decisions that shape land use.

records.quickFact: The Dja reserve is almost encircled by a river — a dramatic natural boundary around one of Africa’s major protected rainforest landscapes.

records.hook: The Democratic Republic of the Congo contains several internationally important protected natural landscapes, including Salonga, Virunga, Kahuzi-Biega and the Okapi Wildlife Reserve.

sections.title: Historical landscapes
sections.body: The Democratic Republic of the Congo contains several internationally important protected natural landscapes, including Salonga, Virunga, Kahuzi-Biega and the Okapi Wildlife Reserve. This range tells a history of forests, mountains, great rivers and changing environments rather than one uniform Congo scenery.

sections.title: Nature and conservation
sections.body: In the east, Virunga rises through habitats from wetlands to volcanic highlands, while Salonga protects extensive central-basin rainforest. The UNESCO register shows how the country’s conservation work is connected to pressures and wider human circumstances. It is a landscape of huge ecological variety.

sections.title: Living cultures
sections.body: The Congo River links regions and cities with histories of trade, culture and communication. Kinshasa is a major centre of Congolese creative life; the country’s music, arts and many languages deserve as much interest as the wildlife of its reserves. No visitor map could represent the country through park boundaries alone.

sections.title: A country much bigger than its wildlife labels
sections.body: Forest conservation is inseparable from the people who live near protected areas and from the histories of settlements along the Congo River. Virunga is especially striking for its altitudinal range, but national identity cannot be represented by a gorilla or a volcano alone. Congolese cities and artistic traditions are living histories, while the huge central forests link local livelihoods to wider climate and biodiversity debates. The best map invites several different journeys instead of one familiar safari story.

records.quickFact: DR Congo’s UNESCO-listed natural sites range from tropical forest to very high mountains — a striking contrast inside one enormous country.

records.hook: The Republic of the Congo sits west of its larger namesake across part of the Congo River.

sections.title: Historical landscapes
sections.body: The Republic of the Congo sits west of its larger namesake across part of the Congo River. Its history and geography should never be mixed up with those of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The capital, Brazzaville, faces Kinshasa across the river, while northern parts of the country form part of the Congo Basin.

sections.title: Nature and conservation
sections.body: UNESCO lists Odzala-Kokoua and the Sangha Trinational protected landscape, highlighting forest elephants, gorillas and habitat mosaics where savanna and rainforest meet. Those are not simply tourist attractions: they are large connected living systems whose protection involves research and local stewardship.

sections.title: Living cultures
sections.body: Congo’s communities, music, language and city culture are distinct parts of its identity. A responsible country profile should leave room for these present-day stories instead of presenting the interior as untouched forest. The river, urban life and rainforest form very different chapters of the same country.

sections.title: Across the river, a different Congo
sections.body: The two Congos share a major river and overlapping ecological regions, but they are independent countries with different capitals, political histories and cultural life. Brazzaville faces Kinshasa across the river; that proximity can surprise people who imagine national capitals are usually far apart. Odzala-Kokoua and the Sangha forests explain another part of the story: some landscapes need cooperation across borders, while local communities have their own histories and knowledge of the forest.

records.quickFact: The capitals Brazzaville and Kinshasa face one another across the Congo River — two neighbouring countries with easily confused names.

records.hook: Russia stretches across both Europe and Asia, so a single capital-city marker can scarcely hint at its landscapes.

sections.title: Historical landscapes
sections.body: Russia stretches across both Europe and Asia, so a single capital-city marker can scarcely hint at its landscapes. UNESCO recognises places as different as Lake Baikal, volcanic Kamchatka and ancient rock art near Lake Onega and the White Sea. Together they tell human and natural histories spanning enormous distances.

sections.title: Nature and conservation
sections.body: Lake Baikal is one of Earth’s great freshwater ecosystems. Kamchatka shows the forces of the Pacific Ring of Fire, while far northern landscapes and the forests of Siberia tell very different ecological stories. The variety matters more than any claim that one scenery represents the whole country.

sections.title: Living cultures
sections.body: Cultural traditions change just as dramatically across this vast geography. The rock carvings of Karelia preserve traces of prehistoric beliefs and water travel; communities around Siberian lakes and Pacific coasts have their own ongoing histories. The atlas should invite exploration of these separate places rather than treat them as an extension of Moscow.

sections.title: Why scale changes everything
sections.body: From Karelia’s prehistoric rock carvings to the shores of the Pacific, Russia’s heritage cannot sensibly be reduced to Moscow or St Petersburg. The Volga basin, Arctic coasts, Siberian forests and Kamchatka volcanic arcs have different human and environmental histories. Cultures, languages and livelihoods vary sharply across that distance. A good atlas should therefore include several separate locations, make clear that the map pin is only one point, and give proper attention to communities rather than treating the whole country as wilderness.

records.quickFact: From ancient petroglyphs in Karelia to volcanic Kamchatka, the same country contains a startling range of historical and natural environments.

records.hook: The United States contains regions with profoundly different landscapes and histories, from Pacific coast ecosystems to interior plains and high mountains.

sections.title: Historical landscapes
sections.body: The United States contains regions with profoundly different landscapes and histories, from Pacific coast ecosystems to interior plains and high mountains. Yellowstone is one of the most recognisable places, but it is only one part of a geographically and culturally diverse country.

sections.title: Nature and conservation
sections.body: In the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, geology and ecology overlap: hot springs and geysers share a wider landscape with grazing bison, predators and forests. Environmental pressures and wildlife movements extend beyond formal national park boundaries. Other American regions deserve their own distinct atlas chapters instead of being grouped under one iconic image.

sections.title: Living cultures
sections.body: The National Park Service recognises 27 Tribal nations with connections to Yellowstone, reflecting a human history far older than its 1872 national park designation. That history helps explain why any place should be understood through both its environment and the people who have shaped and cared for it.

sections.title: Human stories inside the famous park
sections.body: Yellowstone was designated a national park in 1872, but the idea that the landscape was previously empty is misleading. Tribal nations have long histories and continuing connections with its mountains, rivers and geothermal places. Park management also has to consider migrating wildlife, changing visitor pressures and ecological processes that operate well outside legal boundaries. The extraordinary geysers are only one part of the reason the place matters; understanding that wider landscape makes it much more interesting than a checklist sight.

records.quickFact: Yellowstone’s famous thermal landscape has 27 associated Tribal nations; its human story began long before national park status.
